David Mendelsohn interviewed Jim Garrison on May 28, 1989, more than twenty years after the district attorney's famous case. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewYorkDailyNew:
The New York Daily News ran a series called 'Secrets of the CIA,' and this installment profiles Marita Lorenz. Lorenz, the paper says, 'spied on Fidel' Castro. It credits her with an intelligence coup for the CIA inside Cuba. The series packaged intelligence history as newspaper serial, one revelation at a time.

Lorenz's story was told many times, in many venues, across forty years. The Daily News version belongs to the tabloid telling: short scenes, bold claims, a woman at the center of Havana's plots. Readers meeting her here get the outline that later profiles filled in. The installment also shows how the CIA's Cuban operations became popular entertainment while the files behind them stayed closed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RepublicofNewAf:
The New Orleans States-Item reported on August 18, 1971, that eleven members of the Republic of New Africa had been arrested in Mississippi. The arrests followed a shootout in which three lawmen were wounded. The headline prints the group's own word for its members: 'Africans.' The Republic of New Africa sought to form a Black nation in the American South.

The raid on the group's Jackson base was one of the era's violent meetings between Black separatists and the law. The article records the arrests and the wounded officers as first reported. It preserves the local paper's framing of an organization most Americans met only through such stories: eleven arrested, three lawmen shot, a republic claimed inside Mississippi.

Mike Cernovich, the media figure and commentator, sits with Tucker Carlson for a wide conversation. Its announced subjects are the capture of Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and the murder of Charlie Kirk. The third is battling demons, taken in a spiritual as much as a political sense.

podcast-joerogan-5Xq_ZYB8rew:

podcast-tuckercarlson-z8pA2TDXtew:
Catherine Austin Fitts joins Tucker Carlson for a sweeping talk on power grids, bankers, secret bases, and extinction events. Fitts, a former housing official turned publisher of the Solari Report, argues that hidden money shapes the modern West. Her claims reach from finance to underground construction.

Fitts lays out her view that trillions moved off the books to build secret infrastructure. She warns that the power grid is a prime target in any great conflict. the-turn-of-the-screw:
Henry James wrote this tale of a governess and two children in 1898. It first ran in a magazine, then came out as a book the same year. James was an American who lived in England, a master of the fine shades of the mind.

A young woman takes charge of two sweet children at a lone great house named Bly. She comes to hold that the ghosts of a past staff pair haunt and mar the young pair. James never tells us if the ghosts are real or in her mind, and that doubt is the tale's fame.
gikatilla-shaare-orah-hebrew:
Joseph Gikatilla, a Spanish Kabbalist of the thirteenth century, wrote Sha'are Orah, the Gates of Light, as the classic guide to the ten sefirot. The text here is the Hebrew original, drawn from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists. Gikatilla had passed from the school of Abraham Abulafia to the theosophy of the Zohar's circle, and this book is his bridge.

Each of the ten gates treats one sefirah, its names, its work, and the prayers that belong to it. Gikatilla sorts the many names of God into their true order, a task every later Kabbalist thanked him for. The introduction teaches how to pray with the gates in mind. The book remains the clearest map of the sefirot ever drawn.
sefer-ha-bahir-hebrew:
Sefer ha-Bahir, the Book of Brightness, is the first classic of medieval Kabbalah. It surfaced in the south of France in the twelfth century, cast as the sayings of second-century sages. The text here is the Hebrew original, in some two hundred short sections, from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists.

The Bahir speaks in parables of kings, trees, wells, and letters, and through them it births the sefirot, the ten powers of God. Souls pass from body to body in its teaching, and the commandments hold cosmic weight. Its riddles fed the Zohar and all Kabbalah after it. Short, dark, and strange, the book is the seed of a thousand years of Jewish mysticism.
cordovero-pardes-rimonim-hebrew:
Moses Cordovero of Safed, the teacher of Isaac Luria, wrote Pardes Rimonim, the Orchard of Pomegranates, in 1548. It is the first full system of medieval Kabbalah, gathering the Zohar and the schools before him into one ordered whole. The text here is the Hebrew original, all thirty-two gates, from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists.

Gate by gate, Cordovero treats the sefirot, the names of God, the letters, the souls of men, and the channels between the worlds. His mind is clear, vast, and patient, a rabbi building a palace for a wild tradition. Luria would rebuild the palace, yet every student still enters by Cordovero's doors.
vital-etz-hayyim-hebrew:
Hayyim Vital, the chief disciple of Isaac Luria, wrote down his master's teaching in the Etz Hayyim, the Tree of Life. Luria taught by word of mouth in Safed and died in 1572; Vital's book is the record the whole Lurianic school rests on. The text here is the Hebrew original, from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists.

The Etz Hayyim tells how the infinite God drew back to make room for a world. It tells how the light broke its vessels, and how man's prayer gathers the scattered sparks. This myth of breaking and repair remade Judaism and fed Hasidism. Vital guarded the book jealously in his lifetime. Its pages are the fountain of Lurianic Kabbalah.

R. M. Ballantyne strands a sailor in Greenland in Red Rooney, the last of his crew. The tale is set at the end of the eighteenth century, near Baffin's Bay. Nature there seems to keep a workshop for the making of icebergs.
